analysis.one_liner: Requires quarterly oil and gas lease sales on federal land in nine or more states.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being referred to the House Natural Resources Committee in February 2023 and to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee in March, it sat without further action until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force the Interior Department to hold at least four oil and gas lease sales a year on federal land in each of nine states — Wyoming, New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Montana, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Nevada, and Alaska — plus any other state with land open to leasing. It would immediately resume quarterly sales, require a replacement sale whenever one is canceled, delayed, or draws bids on 25% or less of the acreage offered, and expand which federal lands count as available, including parcels nominated through industry expressions of interest and lands subject to drainage. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain guaranteed, expanded access to federal land: mandatory quarterly sales in each listed state, a requirement to offer every nominated parcel, replacement sales whenever a sale is canceled or demand is weak, and a broader definition of leasable land that includes parcels nominated by industry. Supporters also argue more domestic production could help hold down energy prices for consumers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers on federal land

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders the Interior Department to immediately resume quarterly onshore oil and gas lease sales.

Each fiscal year, Interior must hold a minimum of four oil and gas lease sales in each of the listed states — Wyoming, New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Montana, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Nevada, and Alaska — plus any other state with land available for leasing.

If a required sale is canceled, delayed, or deferred, or if no more than 25% of the area offered receives a bid, Interior must hold a replacement sale in the same fiscal year and report the miss to Congress within 30 days.

The bill broadens which federal lands count as available for leasing, including lands nominated through expressions of interest and lands subject to drainage, and requires the department to offer all nominated, eligible parcels in each sale.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost of more federal land opened to drilling: environmental analysis would be pressed onto a quarterly schedule, leasing decisions would be taken out of the department's discretion, and sales would be required even where industry demand is thin. Federal mineral resources would be leased on statutory terms rather than at a price set by competition.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through federal land and review

drawbacks.text: The bill requires a replacement sale if a sale is canceled, delayed, deferred for any reason — including a lack of eligible parcels — or if 25% or less of the area offered receives a bid, forcing lease sales even where market demand for the land is weak.

It requires the Interior Department to offer all nominated and eligible parcels in each mandated sale and expands the definition of eligible lands to include parcels nominated by industry expressions of interest and lands subject to drainage, shrinking the agency's ability to screen out sensitive or low-value acreage.

The bill directs that scoping, public comment, and environmental analysis under the Mineral Leasing Act and NEPA be completed 'in a timely manner' to keep the quarterly sales on schedule, pressuring the agency to compress environmental review of public-land leasing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For supporters, the case is domestic supply: forcing regular lease sales could increase federal-land production and modestly ease energy prices. The drawbacks are substantial: the bill removes Interior's ability to weigh whether leasing makes sense, forces replacement sales even when fewer than a quarter of offered acres attract any bid — signaling weak market demand — and pressures the agency to hurry the environmental analysis that is supposed to precede leasing. It is a broad, blunt mandate that hands the industry guaranteed access to public land at statutory minimum terms, and it never received a hearing where those trade-offs could be examined.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its energy subcommittee, and neither ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matthew Rosendale introduced H.R. 1043 on February 14, 2023, with the bill titled 'To restore onshore energy production.'
The House referred the bill to the Natural Resources Committee the same day, and on March 22, 2023 referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the oil and gas industry did not gain its guaranteed, expanded access to federal leases, and the Interior Department kept its discretion over how much public land to offer for drilling.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public lands and Interior's discretion over leasing

for.name: Rep. Matthew Rosendale Sr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, which took no further action on it; the committee never scheduled a markup or reported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote in either chamber.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal land
industries.note: The bill guarantees at least four lease sales a year in each of nine states plus any other leasing state, requires offering every nominated parcel, and triggers replacement sales when demand is weak — giving companies a guaranteed pipeline of federal acreage at statutory minimum terms. Supporters argue the added supply helps consumers through lower prices; the main beneficiary of guaranteed access to publicly owned minerals is the industry itself.
